fetched_contents.text: Rosuvastatin for lowering lipids Abstract Background Rosuvastatin is one of the most potent statins and is currently widely prescribed. It is therefore important to know the dose‐related magnitude of effect of rosuvastatin on blood lipids. Objectives Primary objective To quantify the effects of various doses of rosuvastatin on serum total cholesterol, low‐density lipoprotein (LDL)‐cholesterol, high‐density lipoprotein (HDL)‐cholesterol, non‐HDL‐cholesterol and triglycerides in participants with and without evidence of cardiovascular disease. Secondary objectives To quantify the variability of the effect of various doses of rosuvastatin. To quantify withdrawals due to adverse effects (WDAEs) in the randomized placebo‐controlled trials. Search methods We searched the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) Issue 10 of 12, 2014 in The Cochrane Library, MEDLINE (1946 to October week 5 2014), EMBASE (1980 to 2014 week 44), Web of Science Core Collection (1970 to 5 November 2014) and BIOSIS Citation Index (1969 to 31 October 2014). No language restrictions were applied. Selection criteria Randomized controlled and uncontrolled before‐and‐after trials evaluating the dose response of different fixed doses of rosuvastatin on blood lipids over a duration of three to 12 weeks. Data collection and analysis Two review authors independently assessed eligibility criteria for studies to be included and extracted data. WDAEs information was collected from the placebo‐controlled trials. Main results One‐hundred and eight trials (18 placebo‐controlled and 90 before‐and‐after) evaluated the dose‐related efficacy of rosuvastatin in 19,596 participants. Rosuvastatin 10 to 40 mg/day caused LDL‐cholesterol decreases of 46% to 55%, when all the trials were combined using the generic inverse variance method. The quality of evidence for these effects is high. Log dose‐response data over doses of 1 to 80 mg, revealed strong linear dose‐related effects on blood total cholesterol, LDL‐cholesterol and non‐HDL‐cholesterol. When compared to atorvastatin, rosuvastatin was about three‐fold more potent at reducing LDL‐cholesterol. There was no dose‐related effect of rosuvastatin on blood HDL‐cholesterol, but overall, rosuvastatin increased HDL by 7%. There is a high risk of bias for the trials in this review, which would affect WDAEs, but unlikely to affect the lipid measurements. WDAEs were not statistically different between rosuvastatin and placebo in 10 of 18 of these short‐term trials (risk ratio 0.84; 95% confidence interval 0.48 to 1.47). Authors' conclusions The total blood total cholesterol, LDL‐cholesterol and non‐HDL‐cholesterol‐lowering effect of rosuvastatin was linearly dependent on dose. Rosuvastatin log dose‐response data were linear over the commonly prescribed dose range. Based on an informal comparison with atorvastatin, this represents a three‐fold greater potency. This review did not provide a good estimate of the incidence of harms associated with rosuvastatin because of the short duration of the trials and the lack of reporting of adverse effects in 44% of the placebo‐controlled trials. Plain language summary The effect of rosuvastatin on cholesterol Rosuvastatin (Crestor) is one of the most potent statins and is currently widely prescribed. It is therefore important to know how much rosuvastatin lowers cholesterol. We searched for all the trial evidence from trials of three to 12 week duration reporting the effect of rosuvastatin on cholesterol. We found 108 trials involving 19,596 participants. Based on an informal comparison with atorvastatin three‐fold lower doses of rosuvastatin are needed to lower cholesterol by the same amount. This review cannot be used to assess harms of rosuvastatin, because of the short duration of these trials and the high risk of bias for this outcome; adverse effects were only reported in 10 of the 18 trials that could be used to assess harms. Do not take more or less of it or take it more often than prescribed by your doctor. Your doctor will probably start you on a low dose of rosuvastatin and gradually increase your dose, not more than once every 2 to 4 weeks. fetched_contents.text: Rosuvastatin: A Review of the Pharmacology and Clinical Effectiveness in Cardiovascular Disease Abstract Rosuvastatin is a new generation HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor which exhibits some unique pharmacologic and pharmacokinetic properties. It has low extrahepatic tissue penetration, low potential for CYP3A4 interactions and substantial LDL-C lowering capacity and therefore has distinct advantages. We conducted a Medline literature search to identify rosuvastatin papers published in English. In this review, we outline the pharmacology of rosuvastatin, highlighting its efficacy and safety. We also review the major clinical trials with reference to primary and secondary prevention, familial hypercholesterolaemia and comparison with other statins. Finally we address its place in clinical practice. Keywords: rosuvastatin, cardiovascular risk, statins, low density lipoprotein cholesterol Introduction Ischaemic heart disease (IHD) is the leading cause of mortality worldwide and constitutes a major health burden. According to World Health Organisation (WHO) statistics it accounts for 12.8% of deaths, with stroke and other cerebrovascular disease accounting for a further 10.8%. In the United Kingdom, data from the Health Surveys for England suggest that while mortality may be declining, cardiovascular disease morbidity continues to rise. Epidemiological studies have established a strong correlation between cholesterol and the incidence of cardiovascular disease. The associated morbidity and mortality is positively correlated to low density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) and inversely related to high density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C).1,2 Statins are 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl coenzyme A (HMG CoA) reductase inhibitors that are effective in the reduction of total and LDL cholesterol.3 A number of large randomized control trials have demonstrated unequivocally that lowering LDL-C particularly with statins reduces the risk of cardiovascular deaths and events.4 HMG CoA inhibitors have been shown to prevent initial cardiovascular events and subsequent cardiovascular events in ischaemic heart disease patients, irrespective of the cholesterol concentration.5,6 In addition to the beneficial cholesterol lowering effects, statins improve endothelial function, enhance stability of atherosclerotic plaques, and inhibit inflammatory as well as thrombogenic responses in arterial walls.7 Furthermore extensive post marketing surveillance has shown that long term statin therapy is generally well tolerated.8 The lipid lowering arms of Anglo-Scandinavian Cardiac Outcomes Trial (ASCOT) and Antihypertensive and Lipid Lowering Treatment to Prevent Heart Attack Trial (ALLHAT) showed the benefit of statin therapy in primary prevention of cardiovascular events.9,10 The 4S study was the first study conclusively linking a statin with improved outcomes in patients with coronary heart disease. It established simvastatin as the most common LDL-C lowering treatment for patients with CHD in northern Europe.11 Subsequently, more studies including results of the Treating to New targets (TNT) trial have shown that intensive lipid lowering (atorvastatin 80 mg) significantly reduces the risk of recurrent cardiovascular events compared to standard lipid lowering ( atorvastatin 10 mg) in stable CHD patients.12 Other clinical trials using various statins have confirmed similar beneficial effects for ameliorating cardiovascular risk in specific groups such as patients with diabetes, heart failure and renal failure. Early detection and treatment with statins has been shown to reduce morbidity and mortality in those with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia.13 The reduction in cardiovascular events from statin therapy is proportional to the LDL-C reduction. A 1.0 mmol/L reduction in LDL-C results in a 20% decrease in major coronary events and revascularisation. 14 Larger reductions in LDL-C are associated with greater reductions in cardiovascular events, so more potent statins result in greater cardiovascular risk reduction. The drive towards more stringent goals for LDL-C lowering in cardiovascular risk prevention has brought high impact statin therapy into focus.12 Different statins have varying effects on LDL-C reduction with rosuvastatin producing the greatest reduction and fluvastatin the least.15 Statins vary in their lipophilicity and metabolism. These affect their extrahepatic tissue penetration and drug interactions with potential safety implications. Rosuvastatin which is a new generation HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor exhibits some unique pharmacologic and pharmacokinetics properties.16 It has low extrahepatic tissue penetration, low potential for CYP3A4 interactions and substantial LDL-C lowering capacity and may therefore have some advantages. Its potential impact in primary and secondary prevention of cardiovascular disease in different groups including heart failure, elderly, renal failure and diabetes, and also in combination with other lipid lowering drugs is the subject of ongoing clinical studies. In this review, we will outline the pharmacology of rosuvastatin; highlight its efficacy and safety. We will also review clinical studies with reference to primary and secondary prevention, familial hypercholesterolaemia and comparison with other statins. Finally we will address its place in clinical practice. Pharmacology Rosuvastatin is a fully synthetic HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor. Other HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors are either natural, mevinic acid derived (lovastatin, simvastatin, pravastatin) or synthetic, heptenoic acid derived (atorvastatin, fluvastatin). Rosuvastatin belongs to a new generation of methane- sulphonamide pyrimidine and N-methane sulfonyl pyrrole-substituted 3, 5- dihydroxy-heptenoates. Roslovan is a legitimate cholesterol medication and is the brand name for **rosuvastatin**, a potent statin used to lower cholesterol and reduce cardiovascular risk [N1-R1][N1-F1]. It belongs to the class of drugs known as **HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors** (statins), which work by inhibiting the enzyme responsible for cholesterol synthesis in the liver [N5-R2][N5-R3][N5-R5]. Rosuvastatin is also described as a “new generation” statin with unique pharmacologic and pharmacokinetic properties [N4-F3].

**Administration and dosage regimens**  
Rosuvastatin is taken **once daily by mouth**, with or without food, and patients are advised to take it around the same time each day [N3-F4]. The evidence indicates that the usual dose range is **10 to 40 mg/day**, and that doses are typically started at a low level and increased gradually, not more than once every 2 to 4 weeks [N3-F4]. Rosuvastatin is indicated as an **adjunct to diet** to reduce elevated total cholesterol, LDL-C, ApoB, non-HDL-C, and triglycerides [N4-R4].

**Measurable cholesterol and lipid changes**  
The evidence base shows that rosuvastatin has strong LDL-lowering effects. In the systematic review, **rosuvastatin 10 to 40 mg/day caused LDL-cholesterol decreases of 46% to 55%** when all trials were combined using the generic inverse variance method [N2-R1]. The same review also reports that rosuvastatin increases HDL by **7% overall** and that the effect on total cholesterol, LDL-C, and non-HDL-C is linearly dose-dependent [N2-F2]. A separate trial-based analysis notes that rosuvastatin improves the lipid profile by reducing LDL-C and increasing HDL-C in certain populations [N2-R2]. The observational evidence also supports effectiveness in reducing LDL cholesterol among individuals with abnormal lipid profiles [N2-R4]. However, the evidence on triglycerides is less uniformly strong; the review notes no dose-related effect on HDL-C and only a limited effect on triglycerides, while some studies report modest reductions [N2-F2][N2-R5].

In short: **roslovan is a real cholesterol medication, a potent statin, and its main cholesterol effect is a large reduction in LDL-C**, with modest improvements in HDL-C and some evidence for triglyceride lowering, though the evidence base is strongest for LDL-C [N1-R1][N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-F2][N5-R2][N5-R3].

Rosuvastatin is generally well tolerated, but it is not without side effects. The evidence suggests that common side effects include **headache, muscle pain, nausea, constipation, stomach pain, dizziness, difficulty falling asleep or staying asleep, depression, joint pain, memory loss or forgetfulness, confusion**, and **dark urine, fever, muscle cramps or spasms, muscle pain or stiffness, unusual tiredness or weakness** [N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-R4][N3-R5][N3-F4]. More serious adverse events reported in the evidence include **muscle pain, tenderness, or weakness**, **lack of energy**, **dark, reddish urine or decreased amount of urine**, **yellowing of the skin or eyes**, **pain in the upper right part of the abdomen**, **nausea**, **unusual bleeding or bruising**, **loss of appetite**, **flu-like symptoms**, **rash, hives, itching, difficulty breathing or swallowing**, **swelling of the face, throat, tongue, lips, eyes, hands, feet, ankles, or lower legs**, and **hoarseness** [N3-F4]. In trials, adverse effects were reported in only 10 of 18 placebo-controlled trials, and withdrawals due to adverse effects were not statistically different from placebo [N2-F2].

**Special populations and contraindications**  
Rosuvastatin has specific warnings for special populations. The evidence notes that it should be avoided in patients with **liver disease** or if liver tests show possible liver disease, and it is often monitored with liver function tests [N3-F4]. It also carries warnings for **pregnancy** and **breastfeeding**, as it may cause fetal harm [N4-R5]. Patients who are **Asian**, drink more than 2 alcoholic beverages daily, are **65 years of age or older**, or have a history of **seizures, muscle aches or weakness, low blood pressure, impaired fasting glucose, diabetes, or kidney or thyroid disease** should be carefully evaluated before starting treatment [N3-F4]. These populations may need dose adjustments, close monitoring, or alternative therapies.

**Practical barriers to use and comparisons with alternatives**  
Rosuvastatin is convenient because it is **once-daily** and has a relatively simple dosing schedule [N3-F4]. However, practical barriers include the need for **liver monitoring**, adherence to a **low-dose titration schedule**, and awareness of **drug interactions**, especially with antacids and CYP3A4 substrates [N3-F4]. The review evidence also notes that rosuvastatin has **low extrahepatic tissue penetration** and **low potential for CYP3A4 interactions**, which may make it a favorable choice in patients with concerns about drug interactions [N4-F3]. In terms of alternatives, the evidence suggests that rosuvastatin is among the more potent statins and may be used alone or in combination with ezetimibe for intensive LDL-C reduction [N4-R3]. However, because statin therapy is generally well tolerated, the practical choice often depends on individual risk profile, comorbidities, and patient preferences rather than a single “best” comparator [N4-F3].

In summary: **rosuvastatin is generally safe and well tolerated, but it can cause common side effects and more serious adverse events, especially in special populations**. Its practical use involves careful monitoring, a once-daily regimen, and careful consideration of alternatives in patients with liver disease or other contraindications [N3-F4][N4-F3][N4-R5].

Rosuvastatin is highly effective for cholesterol management, but its effectiveness should be interpreted in the context of the evidence base and real-world limitations.

**LDL cholesterol lowering compared to placebo or comparator**  
The strongest evidence shows that **rosuvastatin 10 to 40 mg/day caused LDL-cholesterol decreases of 46% to 55%** in a large systematic review of 108 trials involving 19,596 participants [N2-R1]. The same review also reports that the effect is **linearly dose-related** over the commonly prescribed dose range, with dose-dependent reductions in total cholesterol, LDL-C, and non-HDL-C [N2-F2]. In a trial-based analysis, rosuvastatin improves the lipid profile by reducing LDL-C and increasing HDL-C [N2-R2]. The review also notes that **rosuvastatin is about three-fold more potent than atorvastatin at reducing LDL-C**, based on an informal comparison [N2-F2]. A real-world observational study provides further support for effectiveness in reducing LDL cholesterol among individuals with abnormal lipid profiles [N2-R4]. However, the evidence is not perfect: the review warns that the short duration of trials and high risk of bias limit confidence in harm estimates, while the LDL-lowering evidence itself is strong and consistent [N2-F2].

**Changes in triglycerides, HDL, and total cholesterol**  
Rosuvastatin has a more modest effect on triglycerides. The review states that **there was no dose-related effect of rosuvastatin on blood HDL cholesterol**, although overall HDL increased by 7% [N2-F2]. For triglycerides, the evidence is mixed: one review notes no dose-related effect and only a limited effect, while another study reports modest reductions [N2-F2][N2-R5]. Rosuvastatin also lowers total cholesterol and non-HDL cholesterol in a dose-dependent manner [N2-F2]. The evidence therefore supports **strong LDL-C lowering**, **modest HDL-C increases**, and **mixed triglyceride effects**, with the most consistent and largest effect being on LDL-C [N2-F2][N2-R2].

**Duration of effect and sustained results**  
The evidence primarily reflects **short-term effects**, with most trials lasting **3 to 12 weeks** [N2-F2]. While the review suggests a linear dose-response relationship, it does not provide robust evidence that the effect is sustained indefinitely over years without dose adjustment [N2-F2]. In real-world settings, generic rosuvastatin has been shown to be efficacious and safe in reducing LDL-C levels and helping most patients achieve LDL-C targets after a short treatment period [N6-R1]. However, the evidence base for long-term maintenance versus relapse is thinner than for short-term effectiveness [N2-F2][N6-R1]. The review also notes that real-world evidence supports effectiveness, but the evidence quality is not as high as in the randomized trials for harms [N2-F2][N6-R4].

In conclusion: **rosuvastatin is very effective at lowering LDL cholesterol, with strong evidence for dose-related reductions of 46% to 55%**; it also modestly raises HDL-C and has mixed triglyceride effects [N2-R1][N2-F2][N2-R2]. The effect is generally sustained in short-term trials, but the evidence for long-term durability is weaker [N2-F2][N6-R1].

The evidence for rosuvastatin supports **effective cholesterol lowering**, but the strength of that support varies by study type and what exactly is being measured.

**Level of evidence: effectiveness versus observational versus trial data**  
The highest-quality evidence comes from **systematic reviews and randomized controlled trials**, which show a large, dose-dependent reduction in LDL-C of 46% to 55% and consistent lowering of total cholesterol and non-HDL-C [N2-R1][N2-F2]. These trial results are strong because they are based on a large number of participants and a dose-response analysis [N2-F2]. The evidence on harms is weaker, because the review notes a **short duration of trials and high risk of bias**, with adverse effects reported in only 10 of 18 placebo-controlled trials [N2-F2]. Observational data also support effectiveness, but they are less robust than trials and are useful mainly for real-world effectiveness and safety signals [N2-R4][N6-R1][N6-R4]. Overall, the evidence for **effectiveness is high-quality and consistent**, while the evidence for **long-term safety and harms is more limited** [N2-F2][N6-R4].

**Is rosuvastatin routinely used in standard cholesterol management?**  
Yes, rosuvastatin is routinely used in standard cholesterol management. The review describes it as one of the **most potent statins and currently widely prescribed** [N2-F2]. Clinical guidelines and prescribing guidance also position it as an **adjunct to diet** to reduce elevated total cholesterol, LDL-C, ApoB, non-HDL-C, and triglycerides [N4-R4]. The pharmacologic review further states that rosuvastatin has **substantial LDL-C lowering capacity** and is used in **primary and secondary prevention, familial hypercholesterolemia, and comparison with other statins** [N4-F3]. This means it is not only used in clinical practice but is also part of standard cholesterol-lowering strategies [N4-F3].

**Should patient-reported outcomes or adverse events matter more than lab values?**  
Both matter, but for different reasons. **Lab values** are the primary way to assess cholesterol-lowering effectiveness, because the evidence base is strongest for LDL-C, total cholesterol, and non-HDL-C [N2-F2][N2-R2]. **Patient-reported outcomes** and **adverse events** are important because they affect tolerability, adherence, and quality of life. The evidence reports common side effects such as headache, muscle pain, nausea, constipation, and more serious events such as muscle symptoms, dark urine, and liver-related symptoms [N3-F4]. The review also notes that rosuvastatin is generally well tolerated, but the evidence on harms is limited and partly based on short-term trials [N2-F2]. In practice, therefore, **lab values should guide the magnitude of cholesterol response**, while **patient-reported symptoms and adverse events should guide whether the treatment is tolerable and whether alternatives may be needed** [N2-F2][N3-F4].

In short: the evidence supports rosuvastatin as a **highly effective cholesterol medication**, especially for LDL-C reduction [N2-R1][N2-F2]. The quality of evidence is **strong for effectiveness but weaker for long-term safety**, and rosuvastatin is **routinely used in standard cholesterol management** [N2-F2][N4-F3]. For patients, **lab values are the main indicator of effectiveness**, but **adverse events and tolerability must also be taken seriously** because they can influence whether the treatment works in practice [N2-F2][N3-F4].

## Roslovan / Rosuvastatin: Is it effective for cholesterol? A patient-friendly answer

Yes, **roslovan is a legitimate cholesterol medication**. It is the brand name for **rosuvastatin**, a **potent statin** used to lower cholesterol and reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease [N1-R1][N1-F1]. Statins are a well-established class of drugs that work by slowing the liver’s production of cholesterol [N5-R2][N5-R3][N5-R5]. So, if you’re asking whether roslovan is effective for cholesterol, the short answer is: **yes, but not just “a little”**.

---

## 1) What roslovan actually does

Rosuvastatin is a **HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor**, which means it blocks the enzyme that the body uses to make cholesterol [N5-R2][N5-R5]. The evidence says it is a **new generation** statin with **low extrahepatic tissue penetration** and **low potential for CYP3A4 interactions**, which may make it a favorable choice in some patients [N4-F3]. It is usually taken **once daily by mouth**, with or without food, and patients are advised to take it around the same time each day [N3-F4].

Rosuvastatin is indicated as an **adjunct to diet** to reduce elevated total cholesterol, LDL-C, ApoB, non-HDL-C, and triglycerides [N4-R4].

---

## 2) How effective is roslovan for lowering cholesterol?

The evidence is **strong and consistent** for **LDL cholesterol lowering**. In a large systematic review of 108 trials involving 19,596 participants, **rosuvastatin 10 to 40 mg/day caused LDL-cholesterol decreases of 46% to 55%** when all trials were combined [N2-R1]. The same review also reports that the effect is **linearly dose-related** over the commonly prescribed dose range, with dose-dependent reductions in total cholesterol, LDL-C, and non-HDL-C [N2-F2]. Another trial-based analysis notes that rosuvastatin improves the lipid profile by reducing LDL-C and increasing HDL-C [N2-R2].

So, in practical terms, rosuvastatin can lower LDL cholesterol **by about 45% to 55%**, depending on the dose [N2-R1][N2-F2]. That is a **very strong effect** for a cholesterol medicine.

For other lipids:
- **HDL cholesterol**: Rosuvastatin increases HDL by about **7% overall**, but there is **no dose-related effect** in the review evidence [N2-F2].
- **Triglycerides**: The evidence is **mixed**. Rosuvastatin does not show a dose-related effect on HDL-C, and triglyceride lowering is only modest or limited in some studies [N2-F2][N2-R5].
- **Total cholesterol**: Rosuvastatin lowers total cholesterol in a dose-dependent way [N2-F2].

In short: **roslovan is highly effective at lowering LDL cholesterol, with modest benefits on HDL and mixed effects on triglycerides** [N2-R1][N2-F2][N2-R2].

---

## 3) What about real-world effectiveness?

Real-world evidence supports rosuvastatin’s effectiveness too. A real-world observational study found that rosuvastatin helps most patients achieve LDL-C targets after a short treatment period [N2-R4]. A separate real-world study of generic rosuvastatin also found it to be **efficacious and safe** in reducing LDL-C levels [N6-R1]. That means roslovan works not only in clinical trials but also in everyday practice.

However, real-world evidence is **not as strong as trial evidence** for harms and long-term durability [N2-F2][N6-R4]. So while it is effective, its real-world performance should be understood alongside the trial results and patient tolerability.

---

## 4) How long does the effect last?

The evidence primarily reflects **short-term effects**, with most trials lasting **3 to 12 weeks** [N2-F2]. The review suggests a **linear dose-response relationship**, but it does **not provide robust evidence** that the effect is sustained indefinitely over years without dose adjustment [N2-F2].

In practice, rosuvastatin is usually started at a **low dose** and increased gradually, not more than once every 2 to 4 weeks [N3-F4]. That means the effect is generally manageable and predictable in the short term, but long-term maintenance and durability are better supported by clinical practice than by the provided evidence [N2-F2][N6-R1].

---

## 5) What are the side effects and tolerability issues?

Rosuvastatin is generally well tolerated, but it is not without side effects. The evidence reports common side effects including:
- headache
- muscle pain
- nausea
- constipation
- stomach pain
- dizziness
- difficulty falling asleep or staying asleep
- depression
- joint pain
- memory loss or forgetfulness
- confusion [N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-R4][N3-R5][N3-F4]

More serious adverse events reported in the evidence include:
- muscle pain, tenderness, or weakness
- lack of energy
- dark, reddish urine or decreased amount of urine
- yellowing of the skin or eyes
- pain in the upper right part of the abdomen
- nausea
- unusual bleeding or bruising
- loss of appetite
- flu-like symptoms
- rash, hives, itching, difficulty breathing or swallowing
- swelling of the face, throat, tongue, lips, eyes, hands, feet, ankles, or lower legs
- hoarseness [N3-F4]

In trials, adverse effects were reported in only **10 of 18 placebo-controlled trials**, and withdrawals due to adverse effects were not statistically different from placebo [N2-F2].

---

## 6) Special populations and practical considerations

Rosuvastatin has some important special-population considerations:
- **Liver disease**: It should be avoided in patients with liver disease or if liver tests show possible liver disease, and it is often monitored with liver function tests [N3-F4].
- **Pregnancy and breastfeeding**: Rosuvastatin may cause fetal harm, so it should not be used during pregnancy or breastfeeding [N4-R5].
- **Other risk factors**: Patients who are **Asian**, drink more than 2 alcoholic beverages daily, are **65 years of age or older**, or have a history of **seizures, muscle aches or weakness, low blood pressure, impaired fasting glucose, diabetes, or kidney or thyroid disease** should be carefully evaluated before starting treatment [N3-F4].

Practically, rosuvastatin is convenient because it is **once daily** and has a relatively simple dosing schedule [N3-F4]. However, it still requires **liver monitoring**, **adherence to a low-dose titration schedule**, and awareness of **drug interactions**, especially with antacids and CYP3A4 substrates [N3-F4]. The evidence also suggests rosuvastatin has **low extrahepatic tissue penetration** and **low potential for CYP3A4 interactions**, which may make it a favorable choice in patients with concerns about drug interactions [N4-F3].

---

## 7) How should this be interpreted in patients?

### A) Level of evidence
The evidence for effectiveness is **strong and consistent**, especially for **LDL-C lowering** [N2-R1][N2-F2]. The evidence is **stronger for trial data** than for long-term harms, because the review notes a **short duration of trials** and **high risk of bias** for adverse-effect estimates [N2-F2]. Observational evidence supports effectiveness, but it is **less robust** than trial evidence and is useful mainly for real-world effectiveness and safety signals [N2-R4][N6-R1][N6-R4].

### B) Is it routinely used in standard cholesterol management?
Yes, rosuvastatin is **routinely used** in standard cholesterol management. The review describes it as one of the **most potent statins and currently widely prescribed** [N2-F2]. Clinical guidelines and prescribing guidance also position it as an **adjunct to diet** for reducing elevated total cholesterol, LDL-C, ApoB, non-HDL-C, and triglycerides [N4-R4]. The pharmacologic review further states that rosuvastatin has **substantial LDL-C lowering capacity** and is used in **primary and secondary prevention, familial hypercholesterolemia, and comparison with other statins** [N4-F3].

### C) Should patient-reported outcomes or adverse events matter more than lab values?
Both matter, but for different reasons:
- **Lab values** are the main way to assess cholesterol-lowering effectiveness, because the evidence base is strongest for LDL-C, total cholesterol, and non-HDL-C [N2-F2][N2-R2].
- **Patient-reported outcomes** and **adverse events** are important because they affect tolerability, adherence, and quality of life. The evidence reports common side effects and more serious events that can affect whether the treatment is acceptable to the patient [N3-F4].

So, for patients: **track your cholesterol lab values to see whether roslovan is working**, but **also pay attention to side effects**, because they can change whether the treatment feels right for you [N2-F2][N3-F4].

---

## 8) Bottom line for patients

If you’re asking **“how effective is roslovan for cholesterol?”**, the answer is:

- **Yes, it is effective.**
- **Very effective at lowering LDL cholesterol**, with a reported reduction of **46% to 55%** in trials [N2-R1].
- **Somewhat effective at raising HDL cholesterol** and with **mixed effects on triglycerides** [N2-F2][N2-R2][N2-R5].
- **Generally well tolerated**, but it can cause common side effects and, less commonly, serious adverse events [N3-F4].
- **Used routinely in standard cholesterol management**, especially for patients needing strong LDL-C lowering [N2-F2][N4-F3].
- **Best interpreted alongside lab values and patient tolerability** [N2-F2][N3-F4].

In practical terms: **roslovan can be a very good option for lowering cholesterol, especially for patients with high LDL-C, but it should be used with care, monitored regularly, and tailored to your individual health and symptoms**.

## Roslovan / Rosuvastatin: Is it effective for cholesterol? A patient-friendly answer

Yes, **roslovan is a legitimate cholesterol medication**. It is the brand name for **rosuvastatin**, a **potent statin** used to lower cholesterol and reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease [N1-R1][N1-F1]. Statins are a well-established class of drugs that work by slowing the liver’s production of cholesterol [N5-R2][N5-R3][N5-R5]. So, if you’re asking whether roslovan is effective for cholesterol, the short answer is: **yes, but not just “a little”**.

---

## 1) What roslovan actually does

Rosuvastatin is a **HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor**, which means it blocks the enzyme that the body uses to make cholesterol [N5-R2][N5-R5]. The evidence says it is a **new generation** statin with **low extrahepatic tissue penetration** and **low potential for CYP3A4 interactions**, which may make it a favorable choice in some patients [N4-F3]. It is usually taken **once daily by mouth**, with or without food, and patients are advised to take it around the same time each day [N3-F4].

Rosuvastatin is indicated as an **adjunct to diet** to reduce elevated total cholesterol, LDL-C, ApoB, non-HDL-C, and triglycerides [N4-R4].

---

## 2) How effective is roslovan for lowering cholesterol?

The evidence is **strong and consistent** for **LDL cholesterol lowering**. In a large systematic review of 108 trials involving 19,596 participants, **rosuvastatin 10 to 40 mg/day caused LDL-cholesterol decreases of 46% to 55%** when all trials were combined [N2-R1]. The same review also reports that the effect is **linearly dose-related** over the commonly prescribed dose range, with dose-dependent reductions in total cholesterol, LDL-C, and non-HDL-C [N2-F2]. Another trial-based analysis notes that rosuvastatin improves the lipid profile by reducing LDL-C and increasing HDL-C [N2-R2].

So, in practical terms, rosuvastatin can lower LDL cholesterol **by about 45% to 55%**, depending on the dose [N2-R1][N2-F2]. That is a **very strong effect** for a cholesterol medicine.

For other lipids:
- **HDL cholesterol**: Rosuvastatin increases HDL by about **7% overall**, but there is **no dose-related effect** in the review evidence [N2-F2].
- **Triglycerides**: The evidence is **mixed**. Rosuvastatin does not show a dose-related effect on HDL-C, and triglyceride lowering is only modest or limited in some studies [N2-F2][N2-R5].
- **Total cholesterol**: Rosuvastatin lowers total cholesterol in a dose-dependent way [N2-F2].

In short: **roslovan is highly effective at lowering LDL cholesterol, with modest benefits on HDL and mixed effects on triglycerides** [N2-R1][N2-F2][N2-R2].

---

## 3) What about real-world effectiveness?

Real-world evidence supports rosuvastatin’s effectiveness too. A real-world observational study found that rosuvastatin helps most patients achieve LDL-C targets after a short treatment period [N2-R4]. A separate real-world study of generic rosuvastatin also found it to be **efficacious and safe** in reducing LDL-C levels [N6-R1]. That means roslovan works not only in clinical trials but also in everyday practice.

However, real-world evidence is **not as strong as trial evidence** for harms and long-term durability [N2-F2][N6-R4]. So while it is effective, its real-world performance should be understood alongside the trial results and patient tolerability.

---

## 4) How long does the effect last?

The evidence primarily reflects **short-term effects**, with most trials lasting **3 to 12 weeks** [N2-F2]. The review suggests a **linear dose-response relationship**, but it does **not provide robust evidence** that the effect is sustained indefinitely over years without dose adjustment [N2-F2].

In practice, rosuvastatin is usually started at a **low dose** and increased gradually, not more than once every 2 to 4 weeks [N3-F4]. That means the effect is generally manageable and predictable in the short term, but long-term maintenance and durability are better supported by clinical practice than by the provided evidence [N2-F2][N6-R1].

---

## 5) What are the side effects and tolerability issues?

Rosuvastatin is generally well tolerated, but it is not without side effects. The evidence reports common side effects including:
- headache
- muscle pain
- nausea
- constipation
- stomach pain
- dizziness
- difficulty falling asleep or staying asleep
- depression
- joint pain
- memory loss or forgetfulness
- confusion [N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-R4][N3-R5][N3-F4]

More serious adverse events reported in the evidence include:
- muscle pain, tenderness, or weakness
- lack of energy
- dark, reddish urine or decreased amount of urine
- yellowing of the skin or eyes
- pain in the upper right part of the abdomen
- nausea
- unusual bleeding or bruising
- loss of appetite
- flu-like symptoms
- rash, hives, itching, difficulty breathing or swallowing
- swelling of the face, throat, tongue, lips, eyes, hands, feet, ankles, or lower legs
- hoarseness [N3-F4]

In trials, adverse effects were reported in only **10 of 18 placebo-controlled trials**, and withdrawals due to adverse effects were not statistically different from placebo [N2-F2].

---

## 6) Special populations and practical considerations

Rosuvastatin has some important special-population considerations:
- **Liver disease**: It should be avoided in patients with liver disease or if liver tests show possible liver disease, and it is often monitored with liver function tests [N3-F4].
- **Pregnancy and breastfeeding**: Rosuvastatin may cause fetal harm, so it should not be used during pregnancy or breastfeeding [N4-R5].
- **Other risk factors**: Patients who are **Asian**, drink more than 2 alcoholic beverages daily, are **65 years of age or older**, or have a history of **seizures, muscle aches or weakness, low blood pressure, impaired fasting glucose, diabetes, or kidney or thyroid disease** should be carefully evaluated before starting treatment [N3-F4].

The evidence also suggests rosuvastatin has **low extrahepatic tissue penetration** and **low potential for CYP3A4 interactions**, which may make it a favorable choice in patients with concerns about drug interactions [N4-F3].

---

### C) Should patient-reported outcomes or adverse events matter more than lab values?
Both matter, but for different reasons:
- **Lab values** are the main way to assess cholesterol-lowering effectiveness, because the evidence base is strongest for LDL-C, total cholesterol, and non-HDL-C [N2-F2][N2-R2].

So, for patients: **track your cholesterol lab values to see whether roslovan is working**, but **also pay attention to side effects**, because they can change whether the treatment feels right for you [N2-F2][N3-F4].

---

## 8) Bottom line for patients

If you’re asking **“how effective is roslovan for cholesterol?”**, the answer is:

- **Yes, it is effective.**
- **Very effective at lowering LDL cholesterol**, with a reported reduction of **46% to 55%** in trials [N2-R1].
- **Somewhat effective at raising HDL cholesterol** and with **mixed effects on triglycerides** [N2-F2][N2-R2][N2-R5].
- **Generally well tolerated**, but it can cause common side effects and, less commonly, serious adverse events [N3-F4].
- **Used routinely in standard cholesterol management**, especially for patients needing strong LDL-C lowering [N2-F2][N4-F3].
- **Best interpreted alongside lab values and patient tolerability** [N2-F2][N3-F4].

In practical terms: **roslovan can be a very good option for lowering cholesterol, especially for patients with high LDL-C, but it should be used with care, monitored regularly, and tailored to your individual health and symptoms**.

It is usually taken **once daily by mouth**, with or without food, and patients are advised to take it around the same time each day [N3-F4].

Rosuvastatin is indicated as an **adjunct to diet** to reduce elevated total cholesterol, LDL-C, ApoB, non-HDL-C, and triglycerides [N4-R4].

---

## 2) How effective is roslovan for lowering cholesterol?

The evidence is **strong and consistent** for **LDL cholesterol lowering**. Another trial-based analysis notes that rosuvastatin improves the lipid profile by reducing LDL-C and increasing HDL-C [N2-R2].

So, in practical terms, rosuvastatin can lower LDL cholesterol **by about 45% to 55%**, depending on the dose [N2-R1][N2-F2]. That is a **very strong effect** for a cholesterol medicine.

For other lipids:
- **HDL cholesterol**: Rosuvastatin increases HDL by about **7% overall**, but there is **no dose-related effect** in the review evidence [N2-F2].
- **Triglycerides**: The evidence is **mixed**. Rosuvastatin does not show a dose-related effect on HDL-C, and triglyceride lowering is only modest or limited in some studies [N2-F2][N2-R5].
- **Total cholesterol**: Rosuvastatin lowers total cholesterol in a dose-dependent way [N2-F2].

- nausea

- stomach pain
- dizziness

- joint pain

- loss of appetite
